newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Jewish settlers said to meet Arafat in West Bank.
newsitem.headline: Jewish settlers said to meet Arafat in West Bank.

text.p: Israeli settlers from two of the most militant Jewish communities in the West Bank met on Tuesday with Palestinian President Yasser Arafat, a PLO official said.
The official, who said he attended the meeting but refused to be named, told Reuters the participants included Jewish residents of Hebron and the Kiryat Arba settlement.

Arafat has met Israeli settlers before, but such meetings are very rare. The Palestinian leader is still regarded by many right-wing Israelis as a terrorist even though he became Israel's partner in a breakthrough 1993 peace deal.
The official said the meeting discussed the situation in Hebron, the only West Bank town with a Jewish population.
Israel was to have withdrawn its troops from most of Hebron earlier this year but froze the pullout in response to a wave of Islamic suicide bombings in the Jewish state.
Jewish settlers have led the campaign to block Israel's withdrawal from parts of Hebron, where 400 Jews live among 100,000 Palestinians.

Another PLO official said he also attended the meeting and about 13 Jewish settlers took part in the talks in the West Bank city of Bethlehem. He said he did not think they represented the views of all Hebron settlers.
He said the settlers expressed readiness to accept Palestinian self-rule and sought peaceful coexistence with Arabs in the West Bank. He said they posed for pictures with Arafat,
The self-rule Palestinian Authority did not confirm that the meeting took place and the head of the Jewish local council in Kiryat Arba said he had no knowledge of such a meeting.
"I haven't heard about any such meeting and it's hard for me to believe such a meeting took place," Zvi Katzover told Reuters.
Aharon Domb, director-general of the settlers' council in the West Bank and Gaza, also said he had not heard about such a meeting.
Israel agreed in a deal with the PLO last year to redeploy its troops away from major West Bank towns including Hebron, a flashpoint of Arab-Israeli violence.

The Jewish state pulled its troops out of six towns but right-wing Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, elected in May with the support of most settlers, has insisted on modifying terms of the Hebron withdrawal to better safeguard the city's Jewish residents.
The two sides have failed in nearly two months of intensive talks to bridge the gaps on Hebron, each accusing the other of stonewalling the agreement.
